claims.text: Hydrogen spillover on TiO2 enables rapid, low-temperature alloying of noble and base metals.
The spillover-assisted route forms homogeneously mixed noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
The non-equilibrium route can overcome equilibrium immiscibility between noble and base metals.
The spillover-synthesized catalysts have enhanced CO2-hydrogenation activity relative to catalysts made by conventional high-temperature thermal reduction.
The initial material consists of mixed noble- and base-metal precursors dispersed on TiO2.
Low-temperature hydrogen reduction uses spillover from noble-metal sites on TiO2 to reduce adjacent base-metal ions.
The synthesis operates at approximately 150–250 °C in a hydrogen-rich environment.
The route produces a non-equilibrium, homogeneous single-phase alloy with minimal phase segregation.
Hydrogen generated on noble-metal seeds migrates across the TiO2 support.
Migrating hydrogen species have sufficient reducing power to rapidly reduce base-metal precursors at low temperature.
Synchronized reduction prevents phase separation and promotes uniform alloying.
TiO2-supported spillover synthesis yields a more uniform, single-phase structure than conventional high-temperature synthesis.
Conventionally thermally reduced nanoparticles are more prone to phase segregation and compositional inhomogeneity.
The proposed mechanism should be effective for normally immiscible noble/base-metal combinations when TiO2 provides strong hydrogen spillover under reducing conditions.
The mechanism may not apply to supports that do not facilitate hydrogen migration or to systems that already favor equilibrium mixing.
Support surface properties, precursor dispersion, and reduction kinetics might influence alloy formation and catalytic outcomes.
